title: A Letter for the Parish
premise: Silas Nystrom, the reclusive archivist of St. Aldhelm's Cathedral, has built a quiet reputation solving deaths the police dismissed as accidents. When an anonymous client pays a fortune in advance to prove that a murder has not yet happened, Silas and his reluctant assistant, former journalist Mara Voss, discover the client is describing a killing scheduled by the cathedral's own founding ledger — a cipher hidden in the parish burial records for two centuries. As they decode the ledger, they realize the intended victim is the client herself, and that the 'inheritance' at stake is a false identity built on a real murder committed generations ago. In the crypt's locked chamber, Silas exposes the living descendant who has been executing the ledger's terms, but justice must be delivered outside the law: the killer is unmasked before the parish, and the ledger burns — leaving Silas, for the first time, visible.
about_author: Lena Thackeray is the pen name of a former cathedral tour guide who spent a decade cataloguing parish records in northern England. She writes mysteries about people who know too much and are believed too little.

chapters.title: The Advance
chapters.summary: Silas Nystrom's POV. A plain envelope arrives containing five thousand pounds and a single typed request: prove that Eleanor Ashcombe has not been murdered — yet. Silas, who has solved three 'accidents' from his archives, accepts out of professional curiosity. The emotional beat is wary intrigue; the money frightens him more than the request.

chapters.title: Locked Crypt, Open Secrets
chapters.summary: Mara Voss's POV. Mara, Silas's skeptical assistant, tours the sealed crypt beneath St. Aldhelm's and notes the burial ledger's odd gaps — decades of missing entries. She suspects a publicity stunt; Silas suspects a pattern. The beat is friction between belief and doubt as they agree to take the case together.

chapters.title: Eleanor Ashcombe
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. They locate Eleanor, a brisk, wealthy widow who insists she feels perfectly safe and has never hired anyone. Her family name appears in the ledger's margins more than any other. The beat is quiet dread: either Eleanor is lying, or someone else is spending her name.

chapters.title: Three Accidents, Revisited
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Mara pulls the files on Silas's three earlier 'solved' deaths and finds each victim shared one trait: they had researched the Ashcombe inheritance. Someone has been pruning the parish's memory. The beat is cold realization — this case is older and larger than one client.

chapters.title: The Ledger in Plain Sight
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Silas discovers the burial ledger is a cipher: dates of death encode letters when read against the liturgical calendar. The plaintext so far spells a name that does not belong to any corpse. The beat is the thrill of the code breaking open — and the first hint that the ledger predicts a death, not just records one.

chapters.title: A Death Scheduled
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Decoded fully, the ledger's final entry names Eleanor Ashcombe with a date eleven days away. Mara wants police; Silas warns that the last man who went to the police drowned. The beat is rising fear and their first real argument about method: law or silence.

chapters.title: The Client Who Isn't
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Silas traces the payment to a solicitor's firm that dissolved forty years ago — yet the account is still active. Someone with institutional access is paying them. The beat is paranoia inside the cathedral walls; Silas realizes the killer may be a colleague.

chapters.title: The Verger's Keys
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. The crypt keys were signed out the night of each of the three 'accidents.' The verger, Mr. Pell, is affable and evasive, and his family has held the post since 1811. The beat is a cat-and-mouse interview where politeness conceals menace.

chapters.title: What the Ashcombes Buried
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Digging into parish records, Silas finds that the original Eleanor Ashcombe never existed — she was a fabricated heir created to inherit a fortune from a man actually murdered by his business partner, who founded the ledger's cipher. The beat is the theme crystallizing: an identity built on a hidden crime.

chapters.title: Nine Days
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. With nine days left, Eleanor finally admits she hired no one — but she has been receiving letters predicting each of the three deaths, signed with her own grandmother's name. The beat is vertigo: the client, the target, and the ghost may be the same person.

chapters.title: The Second Ledger
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Silas finds a duplicate cipher hidden in the cathedral's stained-glass donor panels, maintained by someone still alive — the entries continue past the historical deaths into the present. The beat is grim confirmation: the murder is being actively planned, not merely prophesied.

chapters.title: Interference
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Mara's flat is searched; her notes on the three accidents are taken, but the cipher pages are left untouched — the intruder doesn't know about them. The beat is violation and resolve; Mara stops being a spectator and commits fully to the case.

chapters.title: The Man Who Drowned
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Silas reexamines the drowning of the last man who contacted police and finds the body was moved after death — the tide pattern proves it. He also finds the man had discovered the stained-glass cipher first. The beat is mourning and fury: the killer's method is patience.

chapters.title: Pell's Confession, Almost
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Cornered, Verger Pell admits his family has 'tended the ledger' for generations — executing its terms when outsiders dig too deep — but insists the current entries aren't his hand. He gives them a name: the cathedral's acting treasurer, Hugo Dane. The beat is a partial truth that raises worse questions.

chapters.title: Hugo Dane
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Dane is charming, generous, and — Silas confirms — the great-grandson of the original murderer, quietly positioned to inherit everything if Eleanor dies before she amends her will. But the ledger's handwriting is not his either. The beat is a false solution that feels too easy.

chapters.title: The Real Client
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Mara cracks it: the advance payment came from Eleanor herself — through the old solicitor's account her family controls. Eleanor has known she was the target for months and hired Silas anonymously because she didn't trust herself to be believed. The beat is betrayal folding into pity.

chapters.title: Six Days, One Choice
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Silas confronts Eleanor, who begs him to simply prove her death would be murder — posthumously — because going to the police is what killed the last man. Silas must choose between the law and the only method that has ever worked. The beat is moral crisis at the story's hinge.

chapters.title: The Hand That Writes
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Comparing ink and pressure across two centuries of ledger entries, Mara identifies the current writer: the cathedral's gentle librarian, Miss Okafor, who believes she is continuing a sacred family duty she was adopted into — the murderer's bloodline by paper, not blood. The beat is horror at how inheritance corrupts identity.

chapters.title: Into the Crypt
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Lured by a forged entry naming Mara as the next death, Silas descends into the locked crypt on the scheduled night and finds Miss Okafor waiting with the ledger and a decision of her own. The beat is the climax's cold opening: two keepers of secrets, one exit.

chapters.title: The Unmasking
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Mara arrives with Eleanor and the parish council, having secretly decoded the final entry aloud to the congregation earlier that evening. Miss Okafor is exposed before witnesses — justice outside the law, delivered by community rather than police. The beat is cathartic, public, and terrifying.

chapters.title: Ashes of the Ledger
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. The ledger burns in the crypt while Miss Okafor, broken but alive, is handed to the police with Silas's evidence at last. Eleanor reclaims her real name — the one her family erased. The beat is release: the cipher's power dies with its secrecy.

chapters.title: A Letter for the Parish
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Weeks later, an anonymous letter reaches the parish thanking them for 'proving the murder hadn't happened yet' — and promising the archive will watch. Silas, no longer invisible, chooses to stay anyway. The beat is quiet, earned peace shadowed by the next mystery.
